# What is a Sprite?

A "Sprite" refers to 2D graphics typically found in 2D games. For example, the Gold Bar item sprite, `Item_19.png`, looks like this: ![Item_19](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4522492/159594962-1a594c3c-cd6c-4741-b60e-f8409461d845.png) .  When making mods, you'll typically need to make a sprite for each bit of visual content you add to your mod. 

This guide will teach you the basics of spriting and how sprites work in relation to tModLoader.

## Sprite Frame
Many sprites have several "frames" within a single image - usually referred to as spritesheets. These are typically used for animation or variation. For example, the GiantBee projectile looks like this:     
![](https://i.imgur.com/jRhab1A.png)    
You can find this texture in your extracted copy of the vanilla textures by finding `Projectile_566.png`. The game was told by the programmer that this sprite has 4 frames in it, so the game knows to split the 96 pixel high texture into 4 equally sized 24 pixel high sections. The game cycles between these 4 frames as the game draws this projectile

Some sprite frames are for variety. Here is the Metal Bars sprite, `Tiles_239.png`, this sprite is shared between all metal bar tiles:    
![](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/9781684c4d69c2de30fc3495148a112bf50207246f4dbf1da36bb5a7afa28620/68747470733a2f2f692e696d6775722e636f6d2f62716f794c71542e706e67)    
Spriting tiles is a full topic for itself, please consult the [Basic Tile](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Basic-Tile#framed-vs-frameimportant-tiles) guide and confirm specifics with your programmer before making tile sprites.




## File Format
Every tModLoader sprite must be a .png file. As long as you don't mess with settings in your program, saving as a .png should work fine. 


## Sprite Making Tools
You **will need** to use a capable art / spriting program. MS Paint (pre-Windows 11) will not work for most sprites you might want to make because it can not save transparent pixels. See [](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Basic-Prerequisites#drawing-program) to find a list of suitable programs. The rest of this guide will use Aseprite in example diagrams, but any of these programs should have similar capabilities.

While the full version costs money, Aseprite does offer a free compilable version that is 100% safe and legal to use. You can compile it by using [this guide](https://github.com/aseprite/aseprite/blob/main/INSTALL.md).

Other spriting programs that are recommended include, but are not limited to:
* [Piskel](https://www.piskelapp.com/)
* [GIMP](https://www.gimp.org/)
* [LibreSprite](https://libresprite.github.io/#!/)
* [paint.NET](https://www.getpaint.net/)

## Vanilla Sprite Resources
Before getting started, we recommend extracting the vanilla sprites to a folder you can easily access. We will be using the `C:\Documents\My Games\Terraria\ModLoader\VanillaTextures` folder in this guide. To do this, follow [this guide](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Intermediate-Prerequisites#vanilla-texture-file-reference). We will be using these textures as guides for sizing and orientation of similar content we will be making in our mod. 

If you just need a reference for how big various vanilla textures are, you can consult this [text file](https://forums.terraria.org/index.php?attachments/sprite-information-spreadsheet-tsv.384515/). 

## Live Editing Sprites

Autoload is a mechanism whereby tModLoader makes some assumptions about your mod in order to simplify the amount of work the modder has to do in their mod. In this Basic guide, we will focus on how Textures are autoloaded because that is the primary interest of beginner modders.

Items, Projectiles, and NPC all need a texture to work correctly. Any one of these without an associated texture will cause your mod to be unable to load. tModLoader can't magically know which texture file you want associated with which thing, but it can make an educated guess based on the pattern it knows.

This is the pattern:

Take the Mod Sources path: 
`C:\Documents\My Games\Terraria\tModLoader\ModSources`

Add the Namespace of the class, replacing '.' with '\\': 
`namespace ExampleMod.NPCs`
`C:\Documents\My Games\Terraria\tModLoader\ModSources\ExampleMod\NPCs`

Add the classname of the class, then append '.png':
`public class FlutterSlime : ModNPC`
`C:\Documents\My Games\Terraria\tModLoader\ModSources\ExampleMod\NPCs\FlutterSlime.png`

In more concise terms, look for the .png file with filename matching the classname of the thing in the folder designated by the namespace of the class.

Basically, just make sure the .cs file and .png file exist in the same directory and that the class in the .cs file matches the filename of the .png file. It is a good idea to also make sure the .cs file matches the classname and .png filename as well. Also, you must make sure that the folder path from the Mod Sources folder matches the namespace (with 
'.' becoming '\\' in the folder structure.)

A visual explanation:  
![](https://i.imgur.com/9z50wHh.png)

# Overview
In tModLoader, we use the `Asset` class to work with assets such as textures (`Texture2D`), shaders (`Effect`), fonts (`DynamicSpriteFont`), and sounds (`SoundEffect`). The `Asset` and `AssetRepository` classes provide on-demand (asynchronous) loading and resource pack support.

This guide shows how to work with the asset system for optimal performance and compatibility.

# General Guidelines
This section is a quick overview of various best practices. See the later sections for more details on each of these topics.    

### Store the Asset reference, not the contained data class
You should always be working with the `Asset` class directly up until the contained data needs to be used. For example, instead of storing a `Texture2D sprite` and calling `spriteBatch.Draw(sprite)`, store an `Asset<Texture2D> sprite` and call `spriteBatch.Draw(sprite.Value)`.

### Preload Textures
tModLoader will request and load textures for most modded content during mod loading. This preloading reduces the need to request textures on demand at the cost of loading time and RAM utilization. 
* These assets are usually accessible in arrays found in the `Terraria.GameContent` static classes, such as `TextureAssets`, if needed.
* If you have extra textures, such as special effects for an NPC or Projectile, you can request them in `SetStaticDefaults` or one of the other Load hooks.
* Vanilla doesn't preload all textures. For Item, NPC, Projectile, Background, and some other types of content unloaded Assets are populated into the fields of the `TextureAssets` class. Using these textures require first calling the respective `Main.instance.LoadX` method to ensure that they are loaded. Vanilla textures without a corresponding `Main.instance.LoadX` are most likely preloaded.

# Introduction
We can use sounds in many places in tModLoader and this guide will educate you on how tModLoader organize and use sounds.

# Sound Basics
There are 2 concepts to be aware of. The first is the actual sound asset. This correlates with a specific sound file, such as a .wav file. The second concept is the `SoundStyle`, which is an object representing a sound asset and associated playback settings.

## Sound Assets

Sound assets can be found in your ModSources folder and in the Terraria install directory. Sound assets can be many different sound file formats including .wav, .ogg, .mp3, and .xnb. For example, [ExampleMod](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/tree/stable/ExampleMod/Assets/Sounds/Items/Guns) has an `ExampleGun.ogg` file found in `ExampleMod\Assets\Sounds\Items\Guns\ExampleGun.ogg`. In your Terraria install folder, you'll find hundreds of sound files in the `C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Terraria\Content\Sounds` folder. These files are .xnb files, which is a special format that you can't listen to directly by double clicking. To listen to these sounds on your computer, see the [Extract](#Extract) section below.

Valheim 1.0 shipped on September 9, 2026. Of 10,801 packages in Thunderstore's Valheim catalogue, 799 have had a new version published on or after 9 September. 418 of those non-modpack, non-deprecated packages now declare a dependency on the 1.0-day BepInEx build specifically.

- attr-no-switch-new | On 1.21.4 and newer Attribute and Sound are interfaces, not enums: never switch on them or call Attribute.valueOf/Sound.valueOf; look config names up with Registry.ATTRIBUTE / Registry.SOUNDS and NamespacedKey.minecraft(key).

# Brief: redesign the Nxeon AI Mod Builder UI

**Goal:** a fresh, flagship-quality redesign of the AI Mod Builder customer UI that drops straight back into the Nxeon portal. Change the UI only: keep the data, API and access rules as they are.

**What the product does:** a customer describes a Minecraft plugin in plain English. AI writes it, compiles it, fixes its own errors and safety-scans it. The customer gets a `.jar` plus a plain-Englis

## Stack (must match)
- Next.js 15.5 (App Router, server components plus client components), React 19, TypeScript 5.8, Tailwind CSS 4.1.
- Repo: `/opt/nxeon`. **Never edit or build there.** Work in a worktree:
  `git -C /opt/nxeon worktree add /tank/nxeon-wt-mbui -b feature/mod-builder-ui-v2 main`
  - Never use `git add -A`; add explicit paths.
  - For `node_modules`, make a directory of symlinks into `/tank/nxeon-wt-release2/node_modules`, or ask how.
- Free RAM on the primary is tight. Run heavy commands as `flock /root/.nxeon-build.lock nice -n 15 env NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=3072 ...`.

## Files that make up the current UI (replace them, keep the same entry points)
- `app/dashboard/mod-builder/page.tsx`: home (prompt box, idea chips, version picker, your builds)
- `app/dashboard/mod-builder/[id]/page.tsx`: one build (live progress, result, source viewer, versions)
- `app/dashboard/mod-builder/mb.css`: page-scoped styles. Every rule hangs off `.mb-root`, and shared portal classes must never be restyled.
- `components/nx/modbuilder/`: `ModBuilderHome.tsx`, `BuildView.tsx`, `SourceViewer.tsx`, `Modals.tsx` (install and change-request), `bits.tsx`

## Data contract (don't change it)
- Types are in `lib/modbuilder/types.ts`:
  - `ModBuildView`
  - `ModBuildStatus` = `queued | planning | coding | compiling | repairing | scanning | succeeded | failed`
  - `MB_STAGES` (the timeline labels), `MbEvent`, `MbCommand`, `MbPermission`, `MbConfig`, `MbFinding` (safety)
  - `MB_VERSIONS` = 1.21.11 / 1.21.8 / 1.21.4 / 1.21.1
- API routes, under `app/api/mod-builder/builds/` (UI calls only, don't modify):
  - `POST /` creates a build.
  - `GET /[id]` returns status; the UI polls it.
  - `POST /[id]/cancel`
  - `POST /[id]/install`
  - `GET /[id]/jar`, `GET /[id]/source?path=`, `GET /[id]/source-zip`
- Install targets come from `lib/modbuilder/install.ts` `modBuilderServers()`, which marks each server compatible or not and gives the reason.
- Access: `lib/modbuilder/access.ts` (`requireModBuilderUser`, a private-preview gate). Keep every page and route calling it.

## Design rules
- Use the Nexion portal look: navy surfaces with the violet, blue and cyan brand ramp (`--mb-grad`: #14c5e4 → #2f7eef → #8c3ae9 → #d623e1).
- Use the portal's theme tokens (`var(--color-tx)`, `--color-tx-mute`, `--color-well`, `--color-rim-*`, `--color-violet`, …) defined under `:root.nx-portal` in `app/globals.css`.
- **It must work in both dark and light theme** (`:root.nx-portal[data-theme="light"]`). Never hard-code dark-only colours; elements that should stay dark in both themes use the `nx-dark-island` patte
- Mobile at 390px must be clean, with no horizontal scroll.

## Overview

VersiCode is the first comprehensive dataset designed to assess the ability of large language models to generate verifiable code for specific library versions. It's a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on version-controllable code generation, addressing a critical gap in existing evaluation datasets by focusing on the dynamic nature of software development, where libraries and APIs evolve continuously over time.

## Dataset Scope

VersiCode encompasses 300 libraries across more than 2,000 versions spanning 9 years.

## Evaluation Tasks and Metrics

Two novel tasks are proposed: version-specific code completion (VSCC) and version-aware code migration (VACM). VersiCode includes a novel evaluation metric, Critical Diff Check (CDC@1), which assesses code generation against evolving API requirements.

## Key Findings

An extensive evaluation on VersiCode reveals that version-controllable code generation is indeed a significant challenge, even for GPT-4o and other strong frontier models. The dataset reveals significant limitations in current models, like GPT-40 and LLaMA3, when handling version-specific code.

## "On Mitigating Code LLM Hallucinations with API Documentation"

The paper explores the challenges posed by API hallucinations in code generation through large language models (LLMs), specifically focusing on low-frequency APIs.

### Key Findings:

**The Problem:** API hallucinations are prevalent, especially among low-frequency APIs, where models demonstrate significantly poorer performance. For example, GPT-4o achieved only 38.58% valid invocations for low-frequency APIs compared to much higher percentages for more common APIs.

**The Solution:** The study introduces CloudAPIBench, a novel benchmarking suite designed to systematically evaluate API hallucination occurrences in software engineering, particularly for APIs from major cloud service providers like AWS and Microsoft Azure. The paper investigates techniques to alleviate these hallucinations via Documentation Augmented Generation (DAG) and proposes methods to optimize when DAG should be used.

**Results:** Documentation Augmented Generation (DAG) significantly improves performance for low frequency APIs (increase to 47.94% with DAG) but negatively impacts high frequency APIs when using sub-optimal retrievers (a 39.02% absolute drop). The authors propose intelligently triggering DAG by checking against an API index or leveraging Code LLMs' confidence scores, enhancing the balance between low and high frequency API performance and resulting in an 8.20% absolute improvement on CloudAPIBench for GPT-4o.

# Paper Summary

**Title:** "On Mitigating Code LLM Hallucinations with API Documentation"

## Key Quantitative Findings

- GPT-4o achieves only **38.58% valid low frequency API invocations** baseline performance
- Documentation Augmented Generation (DAG) improves this to **47.94%** for low frequency APIs
- DAG causes a **39.02% absolute drop** for high frequency APIs with suboptimal retrievers
- The proposed intelligent triggering methods deliver an **8.20% absolute improvement** overall on CloudAPIBench for GPT-4o

The research introduces CloudAPIBench, a benchmark measuring API hallucinations across different frequency levels, and demonstrates that intelligently triggering documentation retrieval—either through API indexing or confidence scoring—balances performance improvements across both low and high frequency API usage.

# VersiCode: Towards Version-controllable Code Generation

## Title
"VersiCode: Towards Version-controllable Code Generation"

## Key Findings from Abstract

The paper introduces two novel tasks:
- **Version-specific code completion (VSCC)** and **version-aware code migration (VACM)**

The researchers created the VersiCode dataset for Python and developed a new evaluation metric called **Critical Diff Check (CDC@1)** that evaluates code generation against evolving API requirements.

## Model Performance

The abstract notes that "version-controllable code generation is indeed a significant challenge, even for GPT-4o and other strong frontier models." However, **no specific accuracy numbers or quantitative performance metrics are provided in the abstract itself**—only this qualitative assessment indicating that even state-of-the-art models struggle with this task.

The paper indicates this represents an important research direction for improving LLM real-world applicability in software development contexts where library versions frequently change.

# Paper Summary

**Title:** "Mage: Multi-Axis Evaluation of LLM-Generated Executable Game Scenes Beyond Compile-Pass Rate"

**Authors:** Hugh Xuechen Liu and Kıvanç Tatar

**Date:** Submitted 8 May 2026

**Key Quantitative Findings:**

The research evaluated 858 generation attempts across four language models (7B–30B parameters) using a four-axis assessment framework. Direct code generation achieved "the highest runtime-pass rate (43% mean)" but produced mechanically flawed outputs with "mechanism F₁ ≈ 0.12". When using structural intermediate representations, runtime success dropped by half, yet structural fidelity improved substantially, reaching "F₁ up to 1.00". The study found no statistically meaningful difference between granularity levels tested (McNemar p = 1.0), suggesting input saturation at that scale.

The core finding challenges conventional wisdom: the researchers demonstrate that compile-pass rates are "anti-correlated with functional correctness" in this specialized domain, highlighting why multi-dimensional evaluation proves necessary for code generation assessment.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Steam's AI content disclosure policy in 2026:

## Key Policy Updates (January 2026)

On January 16, 2026, Valve rewrote large chunks of its AI disclosure rulebook, narrowing what developers must disclose and drawing a sharper line between tools used behind the scenes and content a player actually sees.

## What Requires Disclosure

Mandatory reporting now applies only to generative AI content directly consumed by players. Developers must inform players when AI is used to generate content, from marketing and concept assets to in-game content that players interact with.

## What is Exempt

Developers are no longer required to report the use of AI-powered "efficiency tools" employed behind the scenes. Developers previously faced ambiguity over whether AI-assisted coding tools counted as "AI use" requiring disclosure, but Valve's clarified language now exempts internal workflow tools.

## Developer Liability

Developers retain full liability for copyright and safety regarding all AI-generated assets. Valve makes it clear that developers are responsible for preventing inappropriate or illegal AI-generated content from reaching players, and if developers fail to control these systems, their game could be removed from the store.

## Adoption Rates

As of July 28, 2026, roughly one in five games listed in Steam's store content survey carries an AI disclosure label.

## Key Tools Found

**PixelLab**
PixelLab specializes in pixel art and generates character sprites, tilesets, icons, and item assets from text descriptions, with support for animating static pixel art into sprite sheets. Pricing includes a free trial, Pixel Apprentice at $12/mo, Pixel Artisan at $24/mo, and Pixel Architect at $50/mo.

**Pixela AI**
Pixela AI is a specialized AI game asset generator focused on creating high-quality seamless textures using Stable Diffusion algorithm. The platform automatically generates textures that are perfectly tileable. Pricing is free forever with Pro starting at approximately $10/mo.

**Retro Diffusion**
Retro Diffusion's image generation typically costs between $0.015 (RD_FAST) and $0.18 (RD_PRO). The service supports tilesets, sprite animations, and sprite sheets delivery as transparent GIFs or spritesheets.

**SpriteCook**
SpriteCook generates pixel art characters, props, tilesets, and textures from text prompts with production-ready assets that work with Unity and Godot.

These tools offer API access and different pricing models suited for indie developers and game studios needing rapid asset generation.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about OpenAI's image generation API terms and services:

## Output Ownership

OpenAI's Terms of Use state: "As between you and OpenAI, and to the extent permitted by applicable law, you own all Input and Output. We hereby assign to you all our right, title, and interest, if any, in and to Output." You own the images you generate with DALL-E 3 and can use them commercially - selling to clients, on products, in advertising. This applies whether you use ChatGPT Plus or the API, and there's no revenue threshold like Midjourney's $1M rule.

## Commercial Use

Commercial use is permitted, including resale and use in client work. However, your commercial rights are subject to OpenAI's content policy. You cannot commercially use images that violate laws or regulations, generate harmful or deceptive content, create content involving minors inappropriately, generate political campaign materials, or create photorealistic images of real people without consent.

## Pricing Per Image

For GPT Image 1.5 at 1024×1024 resolution, pricing is $0.009 (low quality), $0.034 (medium quality), and $0.133 (high quality). GPT Image 1 Mini is the cheapest option, starting around $0.005 per 1024×1024 image at low quality.

## Content Moderation

OpenAI's current guidance centers on the multimodal omni-moderation-latest model, which supports text and image moderation. The Omni Moderation API scores and classifies categories including hate, harassment, violence, self-harm, sexual content, and illicit content. OpenAI provides moderation models free through the Moderation API.

Based on my search results, here's a comprehensive overview of text-to-3D API providers for game assets:

## Pricing Per Model Output

### Meshy
Text to 3D generation costs 20 credits for Meshy-6 models or 5 credits for other models. Pro is $20/month for 1,000 credits, which translates to roughly $0.02–$0.20 per generation depending on the model used.

### Tripo AI
Tripo H3.1 text-to-3D costs $0.20/generation, image-to-3D is $0.30/generation, multi-view is $0.20/generation, while premium Tripo P1 models cost $0.50/generation for both text and image inputs.

### Rodin (Hyper3D)
Generation is effectively free and unlimited; you only pay credits when downloading a model (roughly $0.50 to $1.50 each depending on plan).

### Other Platforms
ModelsLab's Text-To-3D API costs $0.0047 per API call.

## Commercial Licensing & Ownership

### Meshy
The free tier's CC BY license means you cannot ship a model commercially without crediting Meshy; for private ownership you need a paid plan. Paid tiers provide full ownership—generated assets are private to your account and fully owned by you for commercial use in games and products.

### Tripo AI
Tripo's Free tier operates under CC BY 4.0, which means you can use generated models commercially without paying, provided you include attribution. If you ship a game with Tripo-generated assets on the free tier, your credits screen or documentation needs to name Tripo, with attribution flexible but visible.

### Rodin
Commercial rights are included on the free tier—whatever you download, you can use commercially.

## Topology Quality & Caveats

### Meshy
Meshy's core mesh reconstruction is optimized for engine-ready triangulated output rather than defaulting to quad-dominant topology. Meshy struggles when input geometry gets complex—small adjacent parts merge together when they shouldn't, and complex surfaces develop scattered holes and broken regions.

### Tripo AI
Tripo P2.0 concentrates on topology, adding quad output, explicit face-count targets, and multiple mesh variants. However, while version 3.1 improves texture quality, the extreme generation speed often results in messy base topology on complex shapes, and professional developers usually need to manually retopologize these models; the Smart Mesh P1.0 mode improves low-poly topology but does not fully replace manual cleanup for hero assets.

### Rodin
Rodin focuses on high-polygon geometric fidelity, which produces detailed meshes suited to further sculpting, though achieving clean quad flow specifically from its output still typically requires a separate retopology pass.

## General Caveat
Before shipping generated assets in a commercial product, check the current license terms directly on each vendor's site—licensing terms for AI-generated 3D content are still evolving, and vendors have changed terms between model versions.

# Retro Diffusion API Summary

## Core Endpoints

The API operates at `https://api.retrodiffusion.ai/v2` (v1 at `/v1` remains supported). Key endpoints include `/inferences` for generation, `/lowpoly` for 3D models, `/edit/tools` for post-processing, and `/pixel-fixer` for restoration. Authentication uses the `X-RD-Token` header with keys starting with `rdpk-`.

## Models & Styles

Four core models serve different needs:
- **RD Fast**: Cheapest (~$0.03/image), speeds up drafting
- **RD Plus**: Mid-tier quality (~$0.06/image) with extensive style library
- **RD Pro**: Premium quality ($0.18/image), supports up to 9 reference images
- **RD Mini**: Low-resolution variants, routing to Fast/Plus

Styles handle artistic direction, from typography to isometric views to Minecraft textures.

## Size Constraints

Images range 12–512px overall, with style-specific limits. Most styles cap at 256–384px; RD Pro typography and small-sprite styles work at 12px minimum. "Most styles" allow batch sizes up to 16 images.

## Tileset & Sprite Features

The API generates wang-style tilesets at 16–32px tiles (`rd_tile__tileset`). Advanced animations transform uploaded pixel-art frames into motion sequences; the rotate feature generates eight directional views from a single sprite. Animations support 4–16 frame durations.

## Low-Poly 3D Models

This newer capability generates textured 3D models with automatic rigging and animation. Pricing scales by size: $0.25–$3.00 to generate, with free exports to Godot, Unity, Blender, and Minecraft formats.

## Pricing Overview

Costs vary by model family: `rd_fast` at $0.03, `rd_plus`/$0.06, `rd_pro`/$0.18 per image. Advanced animations cost $0.14–$0.25. "Check cost before generating" provides free price estimates.

## Commercial Use Terms

The repository does not explicitly address commercial licensing. Full API documentation resides at retrodiffusion.ai; support via Discord or email (support@retrodiffusion.com) handles enterprise and licensing inquiries.

# Meshy API Credit Costs

## 3D Generation Operations

**Text to 3D (Preview):** "Mesh only" costs 20 credits with meshy-7.1, or 5 credits with meshy-6-lite.

**Image to 3D:** Ranges from 20 credits (mesh only, meshy-7.1) to 35 credits (mesh with 8K textures, meshy-7.1). The lite model charges 5-20 credits depending on texture resolution.

**Text to 3D (Refine):** Texture-only operation costing 10 credits for 2K/4K resolution or 15 credits for 8K.

**Remesh:** Flat rate of "5" credits per request across all models.

## Texture Operations

Retexture pricing mirrors refinement: "10" credits for standard resolutions, "15" for 8K.

## Pricing Structure

The platform operates on a "prepaid credit system" requiring users to "Purchase API credits from your subscription settings before making API requests." Volume pricing and custom arrangements are available through their sales team.

## Model Deprecation Notice

Two legacy models are retiring: meshy-5 (October 10, 2026) and lowpoly (October 30, 2026). The documentation advises users to "switch models before these dates to avoid request errors."

The documentation contains no tiered plan structures limiting API access by subscription level—pricing varies by operation type and model selection rather than account tier.

## Key Information Found:

**LogicMods and File Structure:**
LogicMods are placed in the folder ...\Palworld\Content\Paks\LogicMods and consist of three files: a .pak file, .utoc file, and .ucas file.

**IoStore and Retoc Tools:**
Retoc is used to convert mods into the IoStore format, specifically tailored for the GamePass environment. Without the .utoc and .ucas files, the mod often fails to load or triggers "ModClass invalid" errors in UE4SS.

**Unreal Engine 5.1 Modding Kit:**
The Palworld Modding Kit is a community-maintained Unreal skeleton project for cooked Palworld content and LogicMods, where a LogicMod places Blueprint behavior in a predictable Content/Mods/<Name> identity and cooks that content into its own nonzero chunk for UE4SS to discover.

**Toolchain Requirements:**
The pinned prerequisites include Unreal Engine UE 5.1, .NET 6, Visual Studio 2022 with C++ and MSVC v143 14.38, and Wwise 2021.1.11.

**Mod Format Options:**
For LogicMods specifically, the toolchain is the Community Palworld Modding Kit and UE5.1 toolchain with UE4SS runtime, with the main cost being large setup, chunk/package identity, and native/runtime compatibility.

## Key Findings

**Tile Definition Files (.tiles):**
The .tiles file format is used in Project Zomboid modding, where you create a new .tiles file and use tools to add tilesheets to the list. content.content:
# Palworld Modding Kit Summary

## What It Is
The Palworld Modding Kit is a community-maintained Unreal skeleton project for creating LogicMods—Blueprint-based content packages that extend Palworld gameplay. It's not an official Pocketpair SDK but follows the canonical package specification they provide.

## Unreal Version
"UE `5.1` for the current community kit instructions" with specific compatibility requirements. Do not upgrade the engine version, as automatic conversion "can alter serialization, plugins, build files, and cook output."

## What You Can Cook
The guide focuses on Blueprint behavior and assets within a `Content/Mods/<ModName>` structure. While it mentions audio integration (Wwise 2021.1.11), the documentation emphasizes logical/behavioral content rather than detailing specific asset types like meshes or textures.

## Key Pitfalls

- **Version mismatches**: Strict pinned toolchain (UE 5.1, .NET 6, VS 2022 with MSVC v143)
- **Chunk errors**: Your content falls into chunk 0 (default) instead of a unique nonzero chunk ID
- **ModActor naming**: Incorrect folder/filename identity prevents initialization
- **Scope creep**: Primary Asset Labels accidentally cooking unrelated skeleton content
- **Release mistakes**: Shipping the project instead of only cooked output files with proper Info.json metadata

The guide emphasizes testing on clean installations separate from the editor environment.

# Rust Workshop Skin Requirements Summary

Based on the wiki page provided, here are the key guidelines for getting skins accepted:

## Design Standards

**Visual Style**: Skins should appear "dirty and worn" rather than highly colorful or glowing, though some flexibility exists around this guideline.

**Tier Consistency**: Designs must match their item's tier level. For example, a burlap shirt shouldn't resemble metal armor, as this could confuse gameplay mechanics.

## Content Restrictions

**Intellectual Property**: "If you don't own the rights, don't be surprised if it doesn't get accepted," including logos, celebrity photos, and content from other games.

**Text Limitations**: Words and phrases reduce acceptance likelihood since they can't be localized for Rust's global audience. Text-only designs like "ammo" boxes face rejection, but designs where text complements visual elements may succeed.

**Camouflage Patterns**: While accepted, dozens of similar camo variants per item won't all be approved.

## Strategic Submission Tips

- **Target underpopulated items**: Focus on items with fewer existing skins for better acceptance chances
- **Professional presentation**: Include detailed descriptions and multiple screenshots on your workshop page

## Important Note

The provided content does **not specify** texture sizes, file types, the submission process, or policies regarding AI-generated content. Consult the Workshop FAQ or Rust's official guidelines for those technical details.

# Palworld Mod Format Comparison

## PalSchema
**Purpose:** Targeted data edits (Pal stats, items, buildings, spawns, translations)
**Tools:** Editor + JSON schemas + PalSchema/UE4SS runtime
**Cost/Risk:** Schema and game revision sensitivity; minimal download size
**Server/Client:** Supported data changes; affects connected players
**Best for:** "The least powerful format that fully expresses the idea"

## UE4SS Lua
**Purpose:** Runtime observation, hooks, automation, UI experiments, object/property logic
**Tools:** Text editor + UE4SS + live logs/dumps
**Cost/Risk:** Object paths, signatures, timing, and game-thread safety concerns
**Server/Client:** Runtime-only modifications
**Best for:** Function callbacks and conditional behavior without cooked assets

## Resource Paks
**Purpose:** Textures, meshes, audio, and cooked asset replacements
**Tools:** Unreal asset/cooking tools appropriate to target content
**Cost/Risk:** Whole-asset collisions and cooking/version constraints
**Server/Client:** Content delivery; potential compatibility issues with version updates
**Note:** Deliverable is "cooked content, not runtime logic"

## LogicMods (Blueprint)
**Purpose:** Cooked Blueprint actors and event-driven gameplay logic
**Tools:** Community Palworld Modding Kit, UE5.1 toolchain, UE4SS runtime
**Cost/Risk:** Large setup; chunk/package identity management required
**Server/Client:** Requires ModActor lifecycle integration
**Best for:** New Blueprint systems and complex gameplay behavior

## Native C++ / UE4SS Core
**Purpose:** Framework engineering and unavailable capabilities
**Tools:** C++ toolchain, UE4SS internals
**Cost/Risk:** Highest crash, security, maintenance, and review burden
**Recommendation:** Only when higher-level formats cannot supply required capability

# Recipes API Summary

## Recipe Types

The Recipes API supports two primary recipe types:

1. **ShapedRecipe**: Requires items in a specific pattern within the crafting grid. Developers define a 3x3 pattern using character mappings to materials.

2. **ShapelessRecipe**: Requires a specific quantity of items without regard to their orientation in the crafting grid, allowing flexible placement.

## Registration

Custom recipes are registered by calling `this.getServer().addRecipe(recipe)`. Registration can occur at any point during plugin operation, not just in `onEnable()`. The API provides an optional boolean parameter in `addRecipe()` to "update all players with the new recipe" if players are already online.

## Important Caveats

- **Air restrictions**: "You cannot use `minecraft:air` as an ingredient in a shaped recipe"; instead, leave empty spaces in the pattern.

- **Player synchronization**: After plugins are enabled with players online, developers must either resend recipes to players or use the boolean parameter to ensure clients receive updates.

The documentation focuses on server-side implementation but does not elaborate on recipe book visibility, client-side validation requirements, or other player-facing mechanics.

# Mob Goals API Summary

## Capabilities

The Mob Goals API enables plugins to control mob behavior by adding, creating, and removing AI goals. You can assign existing Vanilla goals or implement custom ones to make mobs perform specific actions like attacking players or moving to locations.

## Core Functionality

**Adding goals:** Register a goal instance to a mob entity with a priority level (lower numbers = higher priority):
> "To add a goal to an entity, you need to obtain an instance of the goal and then add it to the entity's MobGoals"

**Custom goals:** Implement the `Goal` interface with methods for lifecycle management (`start()`, `tick()`, `stop()`), activation logic (`shouldActivate()`, `shouldStayActive()`), and metadata (`getKey()`, `getTypes()`).

**Removing goals:** Delete specific goals by key, by type (MOVE, LOOK, JUMP, TARGET), or clear all goals from an entity.

## Example Pattern

The documentation provides a `CamelFollowPlayerGoal` demonstrating:
- Creating a `GoalKey` with namespaced identification
- Implementing `shouldActivate()` to control when the goal triggers
- Using `tick()` to update behavior each game tick (moving via Pathfinder API)
- Declaring goal types to inform the AI system what behaviors are affected

## Notable Details

- Vanilla goals may be entity-specific (e.g., `BEE_ATTACK` won't work on zombies)
- No stability warnings or deprecation notices are mentioned in the documentation

# Dialog API Summary

## UI Components

The Dialog API enables creation of custom in-game menus with:

**Display Elements:**
- Text messages via `DialogBody.plainMessage()`
- Item displays via `DialogBody.item()`

**Input Fields:**
- Boolean checkboxes
- Single-option dropdowns
- Text input fields
- Number range sliders

**Button Types:**
- Notice dialogs (single button)
- Confirmation dialogs (yes/no buttons)
- Multi-action dialogs (multiple buttons)
- Dialog lists for nested menus
- Server links dialogs

## Version & Status

**Introduced:** Minecraft 1.21.6; Paper API released in version 1.21.7

**Status:** Not marked as experimental in the documentation, though some related features like "Datapack discovery" are labeled experimental.

## Client Requirements

The documentation specifies this is for "Minecraft in the 1.21.6 update" onward. No explicit client-side mod or special configuration is mentioned—dialogs appear to function as a native Minecraft feature for compatible client versions, displayed during configuration phase or normal gameplay.

Dialogs support customization via NBT payloads and callbacks, making them versatile for information display or input gathering.

I confirm that rtcheck.py is an eval-only tool, not part of the production pipeline, so I can cite this as a real internal fact. Now I'm planning the structure for ADVANCED-MODS.md, starting with an executive summary, a guide on confidence tags, and a section on cross-game findings like tier ladder patterns.

I'm also outlining per-game sections for Minecraft, Palworld, Terraria, Valheim, Rust, and Zomboid, each covering platform snapshots, advanced techniques, pitfalls, performance notes, and an AI reliability rating (A/B/C scale based on how much human review is needed), plus implications for Cyrus. I'm starting to draft the Minecraft section, covering Paper, Purpur, and Folia's licensing and feature differences.

For custom items without client mods, I'm detailing how Paper's data components API (introduced around 1.21.2+) enables custom item behaviors like `consumable`, `equippable`, `tool`, and `food` definitions combined with resource packs and persistent data containers for state tracking, while flagging the lack of backward compatibility guarantees and conflicts between mods using custom_model_data overrides as key pitfalls.

Since there's no true way to add new block types, I'm covering how plugins like Nexo and ItemsAdder emulate custom blocks using note blocks, tripwires, or display entities, along with pitfalls like block-state limits and anti-dupe concerns for mining speed. I'm also working through GUI approaches using inventory libraries or the newer Dialog API, noting click-handling exploits as a recurring risk, then touching on the experimental and sandboxed nature of custom enchantment registries, and finally outlining mob AI options via the Mob Goals API, Citizens NPC traits, and LLM-driven NPCs that would require external network calls, async handling, and moderation safeguards.

For the remaining systems, I'm mapping out world generation through ChunkGenerator and datapack worldgen JSON, flagging async thread safety as a key pitfall; economy plugins built on Vault abstraction with careful handling of double-spend races and rounding using BigDecimal or long cents; minigame arenas needing robust state machines and cleanup given Folia's broken scoreboards; data-driven quest systems; and finally performance/admin tooling starting with the spark profiler by lucko.

Tracking the surrounding ecosystem too — Paper API, Adventure/MiniMessage, Configurate/Cloud, MockBukkit, mineflayer, and library resolution concerns like avoiding direct Maven Central. Noting recurring pitfalls across plugins: threading issues, PDC copying, player reference leaks, version churn, and Folia compatibility, plus comparing Paper vs Purpur vs Folia vs Spigot for compatibility tradeoffs. Now I'm shifting over to start a fresh snapshot section on Palworld's 1.0 release.

Palworld's post-1.0 server mod system involves config files like PalModSettings.ini and Info.json, flags like -NoMods and bAllowClientMod, and manifest tracking — though the claim that server-side mods only work on Windows dedicated servers conflicts with Linux-based hosting images, which I need to flag as a blocking issue. Modding formats range from PalSchema (JSON-based data) to Lua via UE4SS hooks, resource paks, and Blueprint LogicMods, with major pitfalls being engine updates breaking loaders, the 1.0 update breaking most existing mods, save corruption risks, and UE4SS requiring non-trivial setup.

For Terraria, I'm tracking two distinct ecosystems: tModLoader (stable for 1.4.4, with an active 1.4.5 branch and monthly versioned releases requiring .NET 8) and TShock (a server-side framework via OTAPI for 1.4.5.8, requiring .NET 9) where vanilla clients can connect without needing the mods themselves, unlike tML which requires matching client-side mods. I'm also noting tModLoader's mod structure conventions — build.txt, description.txt, csproj setup, localization files, and icon sizing requirements.

Mapping out the content development ladder for tML (ModItem through ModSystem, netcode, world gen, IL editing via MonoMod, cross-mod calls, config, and TagCompound saving) alongside common pitfalls like multiplayer desync from missing packet sends, texture naming issues, and incomplete mod unloading. For TShock, I'm confirming it's strictly server-side — plugins work through ServerApi with commands/permissions/hooks, but since there are no client assets, you can't add genuinely new items, only reference existing item IDs.

For Valheim, I'm tracking that the game shipped 1.0 on 2026-09-09 alongside Jotunn 2.30.0, with Unity 6000.0.61 and BepInEx 5.4.2351 as the current stack, plus Jotunn's asset pipeline (AssetBundles, prefabs, Mocks, Kitbash) and zone/RPC/ZDO networking details. Pitfalls include Harmony patch fragility against 1.0 changes and ZNetView persistence issues, and for AI guidance I'm splitting tasks into config/stat tweaks via Jotunn's CustomItem cloning versus new models requiring the Unity editor.

Now for Rust, I'm comparing Oxide (2.0.7815, MIT) versus Carbon (GPL-3.0, self-updating, Oxide-compatible but can't coexist), noting plugins are server-compiled .cs with vanilla clients, monthly Thursday updates causing wipes and breakage, and the hook/permission/CUI framework along with uMod's approval process. Key limits are no new models or items beyond existing prefabs and workshop skins, and pitfalls center on hook name changes and per-tick performance costs, so I'm recommending typical plugin work for straightforward tasks while flagging that monthly updates require ongoing hook-diff monitoring.

Switching to Project Zomboid, I'm mapping out Build 42's mod folder structure, Lua scripting across client/server/shared contexts, the server config quirks with workshop mod lists, and emerging Java-based loaders like Avrix. I'm noting asset requirements (32x32 icons, FBX models at 0.01 scale), the recurring pitfalls from Build 41-to-42 breaking changes like ItemType renames and recipe format shifts, and ultimately flagging this as lower-confidence since most training data skews toward the older Build 41 conventions.

I'm now weighing what Cyrus should prioritize adding, starting with version/API knowledge packs per game — this seems highest-value given that most real-world failures trace back to API drift, and doc-augmentation research backs this up for low-frequency APIs, though I need to trigger it conditionally since bad retrieval can backfire; estimating roughly 3-5 person-days per game to build these sheets from actual SDK dumps.

Next I'm considering structured spec/IR before code generation — essentially a "mod spec card" that improves fidelity since compiling isn't the same as correctness — at 4-6 days effort, shared infrastructure across games. Then there's multi-file project support treating config, data, and asset files as first-class outputs rather than just code, with proper file-role tagging and diff-based editing (medium effort). A golden examples library per game, pulled from verified open-source mods and used both for retrieval context and regression testing, looks like strong value for only 2 days per game. Finally I'm mapping out a verification harness ladder — static validators, compile checks, unit tests (leveraging existing test generators), and eventually live smoke testing with a bot.

Now I'm covering dependency handling — a manifest of allowed soft-dependencies with API digests and "requires X" detection in the install UI — plus iterative refinement via minimal-diff edit mode with log-based failure triage, both medium effort but high value. I'm also sketching multi-step planning for large mods using a planner/implementer split with budget caps, a companion assets pipeline for resource packs and datapacks, and outdated-mod detection signals tied to loader and game version release feeds.

Rounding out the list: generalized security scanning for dangerous APIs and AI-generated mod disclosure policy, plus a bounded per-game eval suite of adversarial prompts. I want to rank everything by value versus effort in a table (Value 1-5, Effort S/M/L in person-days, with Games, Evidence, Dependencies columns), being honest that these are rough estimates, and adding a "what not to do" section warning against overpromising features like new MC blocks or custom Palworld models. For the length, I'm aiming for a thorough but efficient document with an executive summary, and for the renders/textures doc I'm planning sections on generator-agnostic principles, asset validation, moderation, and provenance.

I'm now mapping out the per-game asset matrix — covering custom asset types, formats, size limits, delivery mechanisms, and client/server verification needs across Minecraft, Paper API resource pack delivery, item model components, texture hosting with CDN and hash-based caching, and Blockbench model formats.

Vanilla models are cuboid-only JSON, so 3D/voxel tools need to export cuboid JSON rather than arbitrary meshes, and I'm flagging legal concerns around using Mojang's vanilla textures as style-transfer input. For Terraria, I'm cataloging autoloaded PNG conventions, icon dimensions, sprite sheet frame sizing, sound formats, mod delivery via tModLoader/Workshop, armor texture migration, and the challenge of generating exact pixel-grid sprites with AI image models — likely requiring upscale-then-downscale with palette quantization to hit Terraria's specific pixel-art style.

For Valheim, I'm working through Unity asset bundle requirements — prefabs, Jotunn's bundle loading, icon rendering, shader naming conventions, and OBJ model import via Jotunn's utilities — while noting that building bundles typically requires the Unity Editor itself, raising licensing questions for a server-side AI pipeline. I'm checking whether Jotunn's AssetUtils allows runtime loading of textures and sprites directly from PNG files, bypassing Unity Editor entirely, and then moving to Palworld's PalSchema system for referencing existing assets via skin/appearance JSON.

For new Palworld textures and meshes, I note they need cooked UE5 paks via Retoc/IoStore, and that client-side texture delivery means every player needs the install — making this largely infeasible near-term beyond research. For Rust, I'm noting there's no path for custom server-side models, but Carbon's ImageDatabaseModule lets CUI panels display images, which seems like the one realistic channel for AI-generated art to reach vanilla clients, though Facepunch's Workshop skin curation and monetization rules remain murky. For Zomboid, I'm cataloguing asset conventions — 32×32 icon PNGs with the Item_ prefix, FBX models at 0.01 scale, ~128×128 textures, and B42's media folder structure, with sound handling still unclear.

Tilesheets for world tiles need their own packaging approach, which I'm flagging as uncertain. Marketing assets stand out as the lowest-friction opportunity — Cyrus's own listing dialog asks for a mod icon, so starting with listing artwork and Minecraft item icons (16×16/32×32 PNGs) seems like the most practical entry point since they don't need engine validation.

Now I'm sketching the provider interface in TypeScript: types for asset kinds, requests, specs, capabilities, cost estimates, moderation, and results, plus the AssetProvider interface, a registry, pipeline stages, caching, storage, and delivery via a resource pack host. I'm also outlining a per-game AssetTarget plugin pattern for validation and packaging, and I want to check ECONOMY.md to see how Cyrus prices tokens so I can tie in cost control properly.

# Cyrus token economy (design, 2026-10-07)

Branch `feature/cyrus-tokens` (worktree `/tank/nxeon-wt-cyrustokens`). Code: `lib/cyrus/tokens/*`.
Every number below is an admin Setting (`cyrus_tok_*`, editable at `/admin/cyrus-tokens`); the
values here are the shipped defaults (`lib/cyrus/tokens/config.ts`). Nothing in this file is a
forecast of customer behaviour: the cost figures are measured builds, the rest are rules.

## 0. The data this is built on

| Source | What | Numbers |
|---|---|---|
| `/root/agent-notes/modbuilder-preview/phase0-builds.jsonl` | 10 real builds, Sonnet 5, pre-tuning | avg $0.28, $0.08-$0.47 |
| docs "AI Mod Builder: tuning" eval (28 prompts) | service 0.3, Sonnet 5.5 | avg $0.104 / median $0.097; simple $0.066, standard $0.102, complex $0.189 |
| same eval, Haiku on simple | Haiku 4.5 | $0.118/build (more turns than Sonnet 5.5), 1/8 failed |
| build service records on VM 88001 (138 builds, read-only) | auto-routed + Cyrus tiers | Haiku-only auto builds avg $0.068 (n=7); Sonnet 5.5 auto avg $0.104 (n=28) |
| Cyrus tier builds (same records) | `tier` set | Katara ChunkMirror change $0.159; Saka ChunkMirror fresh $0.676 (443 s, Sonnet 5); Saka others $0.055 / $0.304; Yakko SimpleHeal $0.341 (Opus 5) |
| ChunkMirror pre-tuning (auto, Sonnet) | | $0.217 |
| Anthropic list prices (per MTok in/out) | | Haiku 4.5 $1/$5 · Sonnet 5 and 5.5 $2/$10 · Opus 5 $5/$25 |
| Refusals (adversarial prompts) | | $0.005-$0.028 |

Two findings the owner should know (not changed by this work, see Owner decisions):
- **Saka maps to Sonnet 5, not 5.5** (`MB_TIER_SAKA`). The tuned default routing uses 5.5, which
  was cheaper, faster and more reliable in the eval. The one Saka-tier ChunkMirror cost $0.676,
  3x the auto-routed one.
- **Katara (Haiku 4.5) is not cheaper per build than Sonnet 5.5** on simple mods ($0.118 vs
  $0.061 in the eval), because it takes about twice the turns. The economy still prices tokens
  on the real cost, so this only affects how much a Katara build spends, never the margin.

## 1. What a token is

**1 token = $0.002 of measured AI cost** (`cyrus_tok_tokens_per_usd = 500`), times a per-model
multiplier: Katara x1.0, Saka x1.0, **Yakko x1.25** (Opus runs vary more and hold a build slot
about twice as long). A build that reached the AI costs at least 5 tokens (`cyrus_tok_min_spend`).

    tokens charged = max(5, ceil(costUsd x 500 x multiplier[model]))

`costUsd` is the build service's own number for that build (`ModBuild.costUsd`). The token is a
*cost* unit, so margin lives entirely in what a token *sells* for (section 3), and Yakko costing
many more tokens than Katara falls out of the real costs (Opus is 5x Haiku per token).

### Tokens per typical build

| Model | Typical (measured) | Tokens | Big build | Tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Katara | simple $0.068 (auto Haiku avg) | **34** | ChunkMirror change $0.159 | **80** |
| Saka | $0.104 (Sonnet 5.5 avg) / $0.189 complex | **52** / 95 | Sonnet 5 tier: $0.30 / $0.676 | 150 / 338 |
| Yakko | simple $0.341 (measured) | **214** | complex ~$1.18 (Opus 2.5x Sonnet 5 complex $0.47, extrapolated) | ~738 |

Pre-build estimate shown in the composer (`cyrus_tok_reserve_table`, tokens, [typical, high]):

| | simple | standard | complex |
|---|---|---|---|
| Katara | 30-70 | 60-140 | 100-240 |
| Saka | 35-100 | 60-220 | 110-400 |
| Yakko | 100-250 | 200-500 | 400-1000 |

Complexity comes from the existing `lib/cyrus/estimate.ts` feature count (unchanged).

## 2. Game-server grants

    per-month amount = clamp(round5(base + perUsd x monthly price $), min, max)
    initial:  base 100, perUsd 16, min 150, max 750

`monthly price` = what the customer actually paid per month (after coupons/partner discount,
before tax). Prepaid terms: an N-month purchase gets initial + renewal x (N-1); an N-month
renewal gets renewal x N; N capped at 12 (`cyrus_tok_grant_term_months_cap`).

# Advanced mods for the six Cyrus games: how professionals build them, and what Cyrus should add

Research write-up for the Cyrus v6 programme. Compiled 2026-10-08. Research only: no repo changes, no purchases, no sign-ups.

Source tags used throughout:
- **[V]** verified this session from a primary source (official docs, the project's own repo or API, a licence text).
- **[S]** secondary (hosting-provider knowledge bases, news, aggregators, search snippets). Plausible, but re-check before anyone relies on it.
- **[L]** verified locally in the Nxeon repo, the build service or the owner's handoff.
- **[I]** inference or general expert knowledge that was not checked this session.

AI reliability ratings used in each game section:
- **R1** reliable today with guardrails (templates, API sheets, compile and validate loop).
- **R2** works only with an automated verification step plus, for some requests, human review.
- **R3** needs a human (design judgement, binary tooling, or assets the AI cannot author).

---

## 1. Executive summary (one page)

**What "advanced" means.** In every game the same ladder shows up. Rung 1 is configuration and data edits. Rung 2 is scripted behaviour (commands, events, simple GUIs). Rung 3 is new content (items, mobs, recipes, quests). Rung 4 is new systems (economies, minigames, world generation, custom AI). Rung 5 is engine-level work (patching game code, custom assets, cooked packages). AI is good on rungs 1 to 3 and decent on rung 4 where the platform has a high-level API. Rung 5 is mostly a human job.

**The finding that matters most: version drift, not cleverness, is what breaks AI-written mods.**
- Cyrus's own Minecraft build service already learned this. Its reviewed failure-rule file holds 18 rules, and nearly all are API names that changed between Paper versions (`Attribute.GENERIC_*` vs unprefixed, `Material.GRASS`, boats split per wood, `EntityType.POTION` removed) [L: `services/modbuilder/rules/failure-rules.json`].
- Every other game moved under modders' feet in the last 90 days: Palworld 1.0 (2026-07-10), Terraria 1.4.5 (2026-01-27) which tModLoader does not yet ship for, Valheim 1.0 (2026-09-09, "piece categories overhauled", Jotunn rewritten for 1.0.7), Project Zomboid Build 42.20 stable (2026-07-29), Rust's monthly Thursday update. Training data for these games is mostly pre-change.
- Published evidence agrees: version-controllable code generation is "a significant challenge, even for GPT-4o" ([VersiCode](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07411)); valid calls to low-frequency APIs were 38.6% for GPT-4o, rising to 47.9% with documentation retrieval, and badly chosen retrieval cut high-frequency accuracy by 39 points ([CloudAPIBench / DAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09726)); and compile-pass rate can be anti-correlated with functional correctness ([Mage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07342)).

**Honest AI assessment by game (today).**

| Game | Best-supported "advanced" targets | Needs a human |
|---|---|---|
| Minecraft Paper/Purpur | Commands, GUIs, economies, quests, minigames, admin tooling, custom items via data components (R1 to R2) | World-gen tuning, balance, custom blocks, resource-pack art, Folia-safe rewrites (R3) |
| Terraria tModLoader | Items, buffs, recipes, simple NPCs and projectiles (R1 to R2) | Bosses, tiles, world gen, netcode edge cases, IL patching (R3) |
| Terraria TShock | Server commands, permissions, anti-grief, events (R1 to R2) | Anything needing new items or art (impossible server-only) |
| Valheim (BepInEx + Jotunn) | Config and stat changes, clone-and-modify items, recipes, status effects (R1 to R2) | New models and prefabs (Unity editor), new biomes (R3) |
| Rust (Oxide/Carbon) | Kits, teleports, shops, custom UI, anti-cheat tooling (R1 to R2) | New items or models (impossible server-side), monthly-update triage (needs monitoring) |
| Palworld | PalSchema JSON data mods (R2) | UE4SS Lua without an SDK dump, Blueprint LogicMods, cooked assets (R3) |
| Project Zomboid | Item/recipe scripts and small Lua (R2, once B42 golden examples exist) | Models, maps, anything mixing B41 knowledge (R3) |

**Three hard platform facts Cyrus should surface to customers**
1. **Palworld server-side mods are Windows-server only** per community docs quoting the official docs [S: [XGamingServer](https://xgamingserver.com/docs/palworld/mod-installation), [ConnectHosting](https://connecthosting.net/blog/palworld-server-mods-what-works), [gamever.io](https://gamever.io/knowledge-base/server-side-mods-in-palworld-palmodsettingsini-and-the-flag-that-undoes-everything)]. Nxeon's Palworld image is the native Linux server (config path `.../Config/LinuxServer/PalWorldSettings.ini`) [L: `lib/game-control.ts:239`]. Unless that is wrong, most Palworld mods cannot run on Nxeon's Palworld servers today. This must be checked before the Palworld agent's `side` and `reason` strings are written.
2. **tModLoader and TShock cannot be combined**: tModLoader stable (v2026.08.3.0) targets Terraria 1.4.4; TShock 6.2.1 targets Terraria 1.4.5.8 [V: GitHub release APIs]. tModLoader has an active `1.4.5` branch (last commit 2026-10-07) [V], so this will change; Cyrus's version table must treat them as two products.
3. **Rust and Palworld-style "new item" ideas cannot be delivered server-side.** Vanilla Rust clients only show existing prefabs and Facepunch-approved workshop skins [S]. Cyrus should refuse or reframe those requests honestly.

**What Cyrus should add (ranked; details in section 9).**
1. Per-game **version-and-API knowledge packs** generated from the real jars, SDKs and docs, injected only for the target version (the Minecraft "sheets plus failure rules" pattern, generalised). Highest value, medium effort per game.
2. A **structured spec card** (commands, permissions, configs, GUIs, acceptance tests) before code, shared by all games. It also feeds tests.
3. **Golden examples** per game, human-verified and compile-tested, retrieved by nearest match. These double as regression tests.
4. **Multi-file projects with typed file roles** (code, config, data, lang, assets) and diff-based edits.
5. A **verification ladder** per game (static lint, compile, unit tests of pure logic, live smoke test on a throwaway server where the game allows).
6. **Dependency handling** (declared soft-dependencies, compile-only API digests, install-time "requires X" warnings).
7. **Iterative refinement from real server logs**, then multi-step planning for large mods, then companion asset packs (see `RENDERS-AND-TEXTURES.md`).

---

## 2. Method and limits

- Primary sources were fetched with WebFetch or `curl`, plus the GitHub, Thunderstore and Hugging Face APIs, which were reachable. umod.org, pzwiki.net and pzfans.com sit behind Cloudflare challenges; I did not try to bypass them. Where a fact would have come from them, it is tagged [S] and sourced from alternatives (Carbon's MIT-licensed docs repo, a community Build 42 guide, hosting-provider docs).
- `WebFetch` summarises pages with a small model. Facts that mattered were cross-checked against raw files or APIs where possible (release APIs, raw wiki markdown, licence texts). Anything only seen in a summary is tagged [S].
- Dates and version numbers are from release APIs read on 2026-10-08 unless noted.
- Effort figures in section 9 are my estimates for one engineer using AI assistance [I]. They are not measured.

---

## 3. Cross-game patterns

### 3.1 The capability ladder and who can do what

| Rung | Examples | AI today |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Config and data | Stat tweaks, spawn tables, drop rates, recipe edits | R1 when the schema is validated |
| 2 Scripted behaviour | Commands, listeners, timers, simple GUIs | R1 |
| 3 New content | Items, recipes, enchantments, buffs, simple mobs | R1 to R2 |
| 4 New systems | Economy, minigames, quests, custom AI, admin dashboards | R2 |
| 5 Engine-level | IL patching, Harmony patches of game internals, world generators with tuned noise, cooked Unreal/Unity assets | R3 |

### 3.2 Where mods break (all games)

1. **Game or loader update changes an internal name.** Silent failure is worse than a crash: Rust "boots and then quietly misbehaves" after a monthly update [S: [Low.ms schedule](https://low.ms/blog/rust-wipe-schedule-2026), [ConnectHosting](https://connecthosting.net/blog/palworld-server-mods-what-works)].
2. **Client and server mismatch.** Terraria tML, Valheim (when assets are involved) and Zomboid need identical mods on both sides; Rust and Terraria-TShock need nothing on the client; Minecraft plugins need nothing unless a resource pack is wanted.
3. **Threading rules.** Minecraft main thread vs async vs Folia regions; Unreal game thread (UE4SS); Unity main thread (Valheim); Zomboid's client/server Lua split.
4. **Save-data coupling.** Palworld's own docs warn that mods "may cause save-data corruption or crashes" [S]. Valheim persistence depends on `ZNetView` flags [V]. Minecraft PDC data is not copied automatically between holders [V].
5. **Dependency load order.** Zomboid library mods must load before dependents [S]; Valheim needs Jotunn first and then the mod; Paper plugins declare `depend`/`load` in `paper-plugin.yml` [V].

### 3.3 Why the existing non-Minecraft generators need care [L]
The owner's handoff generators (`palworld.ts`, `rust.ts`, `valheim.ts`, `zomboid.ts`) are deterministic templates built with an indentation-aware `code` tag, not model-written code. `palworld.ts` marks 17 API calls as `plausible:`, meaning the name was not confirmed against a game SDK dump (examples: `UPalUtility::SendSystemAnnounce`, `UPalTimeManager` hour accessor, `DT_PalDropItem` columns). Anything generated from unverified names should carry the "Template preview" label until a per-game agent resolves them. The Valheim template already emits xUnit tests for its pure balance maths, a good model for other C# games.

---

## 4. Minecraft: Paper and Purpur

### 4.1 Platform snapshot
- **Paper** is GPL-3.0 [prior research, [V] at the time]; **Purpur** is "a drop-in replacement for Paper servers designed for configurability, new fun and exciting gameplay features, and performance" [V: [Purpur README](https://github.com/PurpurMC/Purpur)]. Purpur plugins use the Paper API, so Cyrus can target Paper and run on both.
- Version lines in Cyrus today: 1.21.1, 1.21.4, 1.21.8, 1.21.11 [L: `MB_VERSIONS`]. Paper and Purpur also publish a 26.x line (Javadocs exist for 26.2) [V: [Paper 26.2 javadocs](https://jd.papermc.io/paper/26.2/org/bukkit/generator/package-use.html), Purpur README branch badge `ver/26.2`]. The service's Java 21 toolchain would need Java 25 for 26.x [prior research].
- **Side**: server-only. Vanilla clients can join. Custom visuals need a server-sent resource pack: `resource-pack` URL, `resource-pack-sha1`, `resource-pack-id`, `require-resource-pack`, a prompt; pack size limit 250 MiB [V: [Minecraft Wiki server.properties](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Server.properties)]. Since 1.20.3 a server can stack several packs and remove them individually [S: [Paper Adventure docs](https://docs.papermc.io/adventure/resource-pack/)].
- Hot reload: not safely. Needs a restart or a plugin-manager reload (risky). `/reload` is discouraged [I].

### 4.2 What "advanced" looks like, and how professionals do it

| Capability | Professional technique | Libraries / APIs | AI today |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Custom items** with new looks and behaviour | Stack data components (`item_model`, `custom_model_data`, tool, food, lore, enchantments) on a base item, store identity in PDC, ship a resource pack | Paper Data Component API, PDC, Recipes API [V: [data components](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/data-component-api/), [PDC](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/pdc/), [recipes](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/recipes/)] | R1 for stats and behaviour, R2 when it needs a pack (art is R3) |
| **Custom blocks** | There are no truly new blocks on a vanilla client. Pros emulate with note-block states, tripwire, or display entities, and use Nexo or ItemsAdder to manage packs | Nexo docs, display entities [S: [Nexo FAQ](https://docs.nexomc.com/general-usage/faq/itemmodels-vs.-custommodeldata)] | R2/R3 (mining-speed emulation, drops, anti-dupe are fiddly) |
| **GUIs** | Inventory menus with strict click, drag and shift-click handling; 1.21.6+ Dialog API for forms (text input, sliders, dropdowns, confirm dialogs) | triumph-gui, InvUI (MIT) [prior], Dialog API [V: [dialogs](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/dialogs/)] | R1 simple, R2 complex (dupe edge cases) |
| **Commands** | Brigadier via the lifecycle API, registered in a bootstrapper so datapack functions can see them; Cloud or ACF in older stacks | Paper Command API, Incendo Cloud (MIT) [V: [lifecycle](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/lifecycle/)] | R1 (but see the 4.5 note about Cyrus's current `plugin.yml`-only rule) |
| **Custom enchantments, biomes, registries** | Registry API at server bootstrap with `compose` and `entryAdd` lifecycle events | Paper Registry API [V: [registries](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/registries/)]: marked experimental; exceptions during bootstrap shut the server down | R3 for now |
| **Custom mob behaviour** | Add or replace AI goals with the Mob Goals API; use the Pathfinder for movement | `Goal`, `GoalKey`, `MobGoals` [V: [mob goals](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/mob-goals/)] | R2 |
| **NPCs** | Citizens with custom Traits, or packet NPCs; dialogue trees from data files | Citizens API [V: [Citizens wiki](https://wiki.citizensnpcs.co/API)] | R2 |
| **AI-driven NPCs** (LLM dialogue) | Async HTTP to an LLM, never on the main thread; per-player rate limits and cost caps; moderation on input and output; fallback lines; prompts held server-side | Bukkit async scheduler; Mindcraft (MIT, 5.8k stars) shows the agent side [V: [mindcraft repo](https://github.com/mindcraft-bots/mindcraft)] | R2; Cyrus's safety scan currently **blocks all networking**, so this needs a deliberate "Connector" design (section 9) |
| **World generation** | `ChunkGenerator` with separate noise, surface, caves and bedrock steps, plus `BiomeProvider`; they take `WorldInfo`, not `World`, because `World` calls can deadlock during generation [S: [Bukkit/CraftBukkit change notes](https://hub.spigotmc.org/jenkins/view/RSS/job/CraftBukkit-RSS/2198/)]. Datapack worldgen JSON is the safer route | `org.bukkit.generator` [V: Javadoc index] | R2 for datapack JSON, R3 for tuned noise |
| **Economies** | Vault or VaultUnlocked as the abstraction so shops and jobs plugins interoperate [S: [Vault explainer](https://mineguard.pro/en/blog/vault-plugin-economy-permissions-explained)]; balances as integers (cents) or `BigDecimal`; async persistence with write-behind caching; transaction logging | Vault API, SQLite/MariaDB with a pool [I] | R1 basic, R2 with races; **balance design is R3** |
| **Minigames and arenas** | State machine per match, arena templates copied per game, cleanup on quit, kick, death and match end | Scoreboard API (broken on Folia [V]) | R2 |
| **Quests** | Data-driven YAML/JSON quest definitions, event listeners, PDC progress | Configurate (Apache-2.0) [prior] | R1 |
| **Performance mods** | Limit entities and chunk ticking, batch work, move I/O off-thread; measure with a profiler such as spark [I] | Paper scheduler [V: [scheduler](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/scheduler/)] | R2: claims of "faster" must be measured, which Cyrus cannot do today |
| **Admin tooling** | Audit logs, rollback, moderation GUIs, Discord bridges (needs network) | Plugin messaging, PDC | R1 to R2 |

### 4.3 Techniques that separate advanced plugins from tutorial plugins
1. **Item identity in PDC, not names or lore.** PDC survives renames and persists to disk; names and lore collide with players' anvils [V: [PDC](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/pdc/)]. The API also warns that data components may break across Minecraft versions, unlike `ItemMeta` [V].
2. **Item models over CustomModelData override stacks.** From 1.21.4 an `item_model` points at an items definition under `assets/<namespace>/items/`, so packs no longer fight over vanilla model overrides [V: [Nexo](https://docs.nexomc.com/general-usage/faq/itemmodels-vs.-custommodeldata), [Items model definition](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Items_model_definition)]. Supporting clients older than 1.21.4 still needs CMD overrides.
3. **Bootstrap-time registration** when the feature must exist before worlds load (commands for datapack functions, registry entries). Requires `paper-plugin.yml`, with classloader isolation: plugins cannot see each other's classes unless `join-classpath` is set [V: [Paper plugins](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/getting-started/paper-plugins/)].
4. **Libraries via the Paper loader**: `MavenLibraryResolver` instead of shading everything. The docs advise against Maven Central directly and recommend Paper's mirror [V].
5. **Tests**: MockBukkit (MIT) for unit tests of commands and events, mineflayer bots for live behaviour [prior research]. MockBukkit builds a ByteBuddy proxy of your main class, so a `final` main class breaks every test [prior local experiment].
6. **Folia awareness** only when asked. Folia has no main thread; plugins must declare `folia-supported: true` and use region, entity, global and async schedulers; `Entity#teleport` never returns (use `teleportAsync`); the scoreboard API is broken [V: [Folia support](https://docs.papermc.io/paper/dev/folia-support/), [Folia wiki](https://github.com/PaperMC/Folia/wiki/Plugin-Compatibility)].

### 4.4 Pitfalls
- Touching world, entities or inventories from async code. Keep async for I/O, hop back to the main thread to apply results [S: skill pages consistent with Paper docs].
- Long-lived maps keyed by `Player`. Key by UUID; clear on quit, kick, death and match end [S].
- Saving in `onDisable` through the async scheduler: the scheduler refuses new tasks while the plugin disables, so the data is lost [L: rule `ondisable-sync-save`].
- `BukkitRunnable` passed to `runTask*` throws at runtime [L: rule `scheduler-bukkitrunnable`].
- Declaring `isEnabled()`/`getServer()` in the main class: `JavaPlugin` defines them as final [L].
- API drift: `Attribute` is an enum on 1.21.1 and an interface on 1.21.4+; `Particle`, `PotionEffectType` and `Enchantment` constants were renamed [L]. These are exactly what an API sheet per version catches.
- Inventory GUI duplication via drag, number-key and hopper interactions [I].

### 4.5 Performance and compatibility
- Paper vs Purpur: Purpur adds config and gameplay options; its extra API is not in Paper, so Cyrus output should target the Paper API and avoid Purpur-only calls unless the customer picked Purpur [I].
- Folia is a different product: most plugins do not run on it unless rewritten [V].
- Current Cyrus constraints in the build service system prompt [L: `prompts.js`] that matter for "advanced": only Paper API + JDK on the classpath (no Vault, ProtocolLib, LuckPerms API); `plugin.yml` plus `getCommand().setExecutor` only (no Brigadier, no lifecycle events, no `registerCommand`); no networking of any kind; no reflection; single plugin per build. These are sound for safety and reliability, and they are the main ceiling on "advanced". Section 9 proposes controlled relaxations.

### 4.6 What AI can and cannot do (Minecraft)
- **R1:** commands, listeners, config-driven features, simple GUIs, quests from data, many admin tools. Compile-and-scan catches most failures.
- **R2:** custom items with resource packs, economies, minigames, mob goals, datapack worldgen. Needs spec confirmation, tests and a live smoke test.
- **R3:** economy balance and game feel, world-gen tuning, custom blocks, Folia migration, resource-pack art, performance claims.
- Nothing in Paper adds new blocks or items on a vanilla client; say so plainly in the UI [prior research].

## 5. Terraria: tModLoader and TShock

### 5.1 Platform snapshot [V: GitHub APIs, 2026-10-08]
- **tModLoader** is MIT. Stable `v2026.08.3.0` (2026-10-01) targets **Terraria 1.4.4**; a preview `v2026.09.2.1` is also 1.4.4. A `1.4.5` branch is under active development (commits on 2026-10-07). Monthly-style version tags and a long "Update Migration Guide" with one section per month show a fast breaking-change cadence, and `tModPorter` exists to help port [V: [wiki](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Update-Migration-Guide)]. Needs the **.NET 8 SDK** (.NET 9 and 10 explicitly "will not work") [V: [developer guide](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/tModLoader-guide-for-developers)].
- **TShock** (server mod, vanilla clients can join) `6.2.1` (2026-09-27) targets **Terraria 1.4.5.8**; earlier 6.x covered 1.4.5.5 and 1.4.5.6; 5.2.x covered 1.4.4.9 [V]. Built on OTAPI; building needs the .NET 9 SDK [V: [TShock README](https://github.com/Pryaxis/TShock)].
- **Sides.** tML content mods must be on server **and** every client at the same versions; a mismatch blocks joining; clients are usually prompted to download missing mods [S: [FragNet](https://kb.fragnet.net/Games/Terraria/How_to_add_mods_to_your_tModLoader_server/), [Falix](https://client.falixnodes.net/guides/game-servers/terraria-tmodloader-mods), several others]. TShock needs nothing on the client [I, consistent with its design as a server plugin host].
- **Server install for tML:** `.tmod` files plus `enabled.json` in the server's Mods folder, or a management script that installs from a Workshop-exported `install.txt` [V: [Starting a modded server](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Starting-a-modded-server); the page notes it is outdated for 1.4.4 dedicated servers and points to the `DedicatedServerUtils` readme].

### 5.2 Mod anatomy (tML) [V: [Basic Modding Guide](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Basic-tModLoader-Modding-Guide)]
`build.txt` (display name, author, version), `description.txt`, `.csproj`, one `Mod` class, content classes (`ModItem`, `ModNPC`, `ModProjectile`, `ModTile`, `ModBuff`, `ModPlayer`, `ModSystem`, `GlobalItem`, ...), localisation in `Localization/en-US_Mods.<Name>.hjson`, `icon.png` (80x80) and `icon_small.png` (30x30). Output is a `.tmod` file built with Build + Reload.

**Textures are autoloaded by class path:** a PNG next to the `.cs` with the same name as the class. "Items, Projectiles, and NPC all need a texture... any one of these without an associated texture will cause your mod to be unable to load" [V: [Basic Autoload](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Basic-Autoload)]. This is a concrete hazard for any AI generator that emits an item without art.

### 5.3 What advanced looks like (tML)

| Capability | Technique | AI today |
|---|---|---|
| Weapons, armour, accessories, buffs | `ModItem` hooks, `ModPlayer` for set bonuses, `GlobalItem` to change vanilla; recipes in `ModItem.AddRecipes` or `ModSystem.AddRecipes` [V: [recipes](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Basic-Recipes)] | R1 to R2 |
| Minions and projectiles | Custom AI via `ModProjectile.AI`, buff-plus-minion pattern | R2 |
| NPCs and bosses | `ModNPC` AI states, spawn conditions, loot via `ModifyNPCLoot` | R2 simple, R3 boss fights (balance and telegraphing) |
| Tiles and tile entities | Framed tiles, `ModTileEntity`, placement and mining rules | R3 (sprite frames and hitboxes are fussy) |
| World generation | `ModSystem.ModifyWorldGenTasks`, reference the vanilla step list [V: wiki index lists World Generation and Vanilla World Generation Steps] | R3 |
| Custom UI | `UIState` via `ModSystem` interface layers | R2/R3 |
| Config | `ModConfig` (JSON-backed, server-synced) | R1 |
| Saving data | `TagCompound` in `SaveData/LoadData` [V: wiki index "Saving and loading"] | R1 |
| Cross-mod support | `Mod.Call`, weak references [V: wiki index "Expert Cross Mod Content"] | R2 |
| Patching vanilla | IL editing and detours with MonoMod [V: wiki index "Expert IL Editing", "Advanced Detouring"] | R3, and it breaks every Terraria update |
| Shaders | Armour dyes and screen shaders [V: wiki index] | R3 |

### 5.4 Netcode (the usual multiplayer killer)
- Three flows: client to server to clients, client to server, server to client. Use `ModPacket` and `HandlePacket`; keep packets small; prefer deterministic logic so less must be sent [V: [Intermediate netcode](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/wiki/Intermediate-netcode)].
- "If a mod is actually buggy during multiplayer, it is often because they do not send packets at all and clients aren't synchronized" [V, same page]. AI-generated tML mods that were only reasoned about in single player will desync. A validator can at least flag state mutated in `Update` hooks with no sync call.

### 5.5 TShock (server plugin) techniques
- Plugins are .NET DLLs on OTAPI; "you have direct access to all public fields in the `Terraria` namespace" [V: TShock README]. Typical advanced work: command suites, permission groups, region protection, event rewards, anti-cheat tuning, scheduled events, per-group item rules.
- It cannot add items or art (vanilla clients do not have them), so "custom item" requests belong to tML, not TShock.
- Decompiled server sources are maintained by the TShock team for contributors [V README]; they are proprietary-derived, so Cyrus must not ship them.

### 5.6 Pitfalls
- Wrong .NET SDK (8 vs 9) [V]. Texture and class name mismatches [V]. Missing localisation keys [I].
- "Mod not fully unloaded" memory leaks from static references; the wiki has a dedicated page [V: index link].
- Packet bloat and desync [V]. IL patches breaking on every update [V by cadence].
- The two ecosystems target different Terraria versions today [V]. A tML mod on a 1.4.5 TShock server is not a thing.
- Mods that add content change world and player files, so removing a mod can orphan items or tiles [I].

### 5.7 What AI can and cannot do (Terraria)
- **R1:** a `ModItem` with stats and a recipe, buffs, simple `ModConfig`, TShock commands. The official ExampleMod (MIT) is a strong golden reference; tML `ExampleMod` ships in the repo [V: [ExampleMod](https://github.com/tModLoader/tModLoader/tree/stable/ExampleMod)].
- **R2:** projectiles, minions, simple NPCs, UI panels. Needs compile against the real tML assemblies and a load test.
- **R3:** bosses, tiles, world gen, IL editing, netcode design, sprite frames. A compile check cannot tell if the game plays well.
- Verification: tML can run a headless dedicated server on Linux with the management script [V], so a load-and-join smoke test is plausible. It needs the game's licensed files via SteamCMD, which Cyrus must not redistribute; the Terraria agent owns this call.
